text: Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through.
Now there was a man named Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, and he was rich.

versions.text: There was a man there named Zacchaeus; he was a chief tax collector, and he was rich.
versions.explanation: "There was a man there" is clumsy for oral reading with the doubled "there," and the sentence is smoother without the second full clause.

text: He was trying to see who Jesus was, but he could not because of the crowd, since he was short.
So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see him, since Jesus was about to pass that way.
When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and said to him, "Zacchaeus, hurry down, for today I must stay at your house."
So he hurried down and welcomed him with joy.
When they all saw it, they began to grumble, "He has gone in to stay with a sinful man."
But Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord, "Look, Lord, I am giving half of what I own to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone of anything, I am paying it back four times over."
Jesus said to him, "Today salvation has come to this house, since he too is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost."
As they were listening to this, he went on to tell a parable, because he was near Jerusalem and they thought the kingdom of God was going to appear at any moment.
So he said: "A man of noble birth went to a distant country to be appointed king and then to return.
He called ten of his servants, gave them ten minas, and said to them, 'Put this money to work until I come back.'
But his countrymen hated him, and they sent a delegation after him to say, 'We do not want this man to be our king.'
When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered the servants to whom he had given the money to be called in, so he could find out what they had gained by trading.
The first came forward and said, 'Master, your mina has earned ten more.'
He said to him, 'Well done, good servant! Since you have been faithful with a very small thing, take charge of ten cities.'
The second came and said, 'Your mina, master, has made five more.'
He said to this one as well, 'You too—take charge of five cities.'

versions.text: To him he said, 'You take charge of five cities.'
versions.explanation: The Greek καὶ σὺ ("you also/you too") is not rendered, losing the parallel with the first servant's reward. The added emphasis also improves the oral rhythm.

versions.text: To this one he said, 'You too—take charge of five cities.'
versions.explanation: The Greek has two occurrences of καί: καὶ τούτῳ ('to this one also/as well') and καὶ σύ ('you too'). The current rendering captures the second but drops the first, which marks the parallel between the master's two responses. 'He said to this one as well' also flows more naturally for oral reading than the fronted 'To this one he said.'

text: Then another came and said, 'Master, here is your mina. I kept it laid away in a cloth,
because I was afraid of you. You are a harsh man: you take what you did not deposit and reap what you did not sow.'
He said to him, 'Out of your own mouth I judge you, you wicked servant. You knew that I am a harsh man, taking what I did not deposit and reaping what I did not sow?
Then why didn't you put my money on deposit, so that when I came back I could have collected it with interest?'
Then he said to those standing there, 'Take the mina away from him and give it to the one who has ten.'
They said to him, 'Master, he already has ten minas!'
'I tell you, to everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who has nothing, even what he has will be taken away.
But as for these enemies of mine who did not want me to be their king—bring them here and slaughter them in front of me.'"
After saying this, Jesus went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.
As he approached Bethphage and Bethany at the mountain called the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples,

versions.text: As he approached Bethphage and Bethany at the hill called the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples,
versions.explanation: "The hill called the Mount of Olives" is internally inconsistent (hill/mount) and reads awkwardly; ὄρος is elsewhere in this chapter (v. 37) rendered "Mount," so keeping the same term aids consistency for hearers.

text: saying, "Go to the village ahead of you. As you enter it, you will find a colt tied there, which no one has ever ridden. Untie it and bring it here.
If anyone asks you, 'Why are you untying it?' say this: 'The Lord needs it.'"
Those who were sent went and found it just as he had told them.
As they were untying the colt, its owners asked them, "Why are you untying the colt?"
They answered, "The Lord needs it."
They brought it to Jesus, threw their cloaks on the colt, and helped him onto it.
As he rode along, people spread their cloaks on the road.
When he came near the place where the road goes down the Mount of Olives, the whole crowd of disciples began joyfully to praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works they had seen:
"Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!"
Some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, "Teacher, rebuke your disciples!"
He answered, "I tell you, if they keep silent, the stones will cry out."
As he came near and saw the city, he wept over it,
saying, "If you had only known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes.
The days will come upon you when your enemies will throw up a siege wall against you, surround you, and hem you in on every side.
They will level you to the ground, you and your children within your walls, and they will not leave one stone on another in you, because you did not recognize the time of God's coming to you."
Then he entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling.
He said to them, "It is written: 'My house will be a house of prayer'—but you have made it a den of robbers."
Every day he was teaching in the temple. But the chief priests, the scribes, and the leaders of the people were looking for a way to destroy him,
yet they could not find any way to do it, because all the people hung on his every word.
